Injectivity of $f$ gives injectivity of $g$, and $g(0)=\tfrac{1}{f(0)}=1$.

Rewrite the given equation. The right-hand side is
$$\frac{f(x)f(y)}{f(x)+f(y)}=\frac{1}{\tfrac{1}{f(x)}+\tfrac{1}{f(y)}}=\frac{1}{g(x)+g(y)},$$
so taking reciprocals of both sides yields the Cauchy-type equation
$$\boxed{g\!\big(x+g(y)\big)=g(x)+g(y)}\qquad\text{for all }x,y\ge 0.\tag{$\ast$}$$

**Step 1.** Set $y=0$ in $(\ast)$, using $g(0)=1$:
$$g(x+1)=g(x)+1\qquad\text{for all }x\ge 0.\tag{1}$$

**Step 2.** Set $x=0$ in $(\ast)$, using $g(0)=1$:
$$g(g(y))=1+g(y)\qquad\text{for all }y\ge 0.\tag{2}$$

**Step 3 (key).** From (1) with $x=y$ we have $g(y+1)=g(y)+1=1+g(y)$. Comparing with (2):
$$g(g(y))=g(y+1)\qquad\text{for all }y\ge 0.$$
Since $g$ is **injective**, equality of the outputs forces equality of the inputs:
$$g(y)=y+1\qquad\text{for all }y\ge 0.$$

Therefore
$$f(y)=\frac{1}{g(y)}=\frac{1}{y+1}.$$

$$f\!\left(x+\tfrac{1}{f(y)}\right)=f(x+y+1)=\frac{1}{x+y+2},$$
while the right-hand side is
$$\frac{f(x)f(y)}{f(x)+f(y)}=\frac{\tfrac{1}{(x+1)(y+1)}}{\tfrac{1}{x+1}+\tfrac{1}{y+1}}=\frac{1}{(x+1)+(y+1)}=\frac{1}{x+y+2}.\quad\checkmark$$

**Conclusion.**
$$f(2012)=\frac{1}{2012+1}=\boxed{\dfrac{1}{2013}}.$$
